plot_extraction.response_text:
Topham, an educated but disgraced and impoverished man, performs nearly all the work for Rudolph Starkey’s correspondence-tuition business in exchange for mere room and board. Exploited, overworked, and treated contemptuously, he remains only because he fears homelessness.

When Abraham Wigmore, a prosperous middle-aged fruiterer and one of the correspondence pupils, visits unexpectedly, Topham impersonates Starkey. Wigmore reveals that his daughters have married into a higher social class and seem ashamed of his humble occupation. Hoping to gain respectability, he wants to retire from trade, pursue an education, and eventually become a curate.

Recognizing an escape from servitude, Topham persuades Wigmore that intensive private tuition could prepare him for ordination. He accepts a position as Wigmore’s resident tutor at a generous salary, takes an advance, and leaves Starkey without warning, repaying a recently lent sixpence with ironic gratitude. He also sends Starkey a forged letter claiming that Wigmore is too ill to continue studying.

Later, Topham confesses the deception to Wigmore, who decides that Starkey deserved it. Topham diligently educates his new employer and consoles himself that his trick not only rescued him from exploitation but also protected Wigmore from a dishonest tutor and may genuinely help him enter the Church.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a clear, controlled late-Victorian/Edwardian realist style, combining social observation with dry moral comedy. Its prose is formal but accessible, with an omniscient narrator who moves easily between outward description, compressed biography, psychological analysis, and ironic commentary. The opening is economical and visual: two men, their contrasting clothes and postures, and a table covered with work immediately establish the unequal relationship. Material details such as the cigarette, wooden penholder, sixpenny piece, papers, advertisements, and shabby lodging carry much of the social meaning. Poverty and status are rendered through concrete objects rather than elaborate scenic description.

The narration is strongly character-centred. It frequently explains motives and contradictions in compact, balanced sentences, especially when describing Starkey’s self-deception: his laziness is recast in his own mind as unrewarded industry, and his selfishness as unworldliness. This technique creates irony by placing a character’s flattering self-image beside the narrator’s blunt judgement. Aphoristic formulations—such as the observation that Starkey “did everything by halves and snarl[ed] over the ineffectual results”—give the prose satirical sharpness. The narrator is authoritative and morally discriminating, but not solemn; the final remark, “Such thoughts are very consoling,” quietly exposes Topham’s rationalisation without explicitly condemning him.

Sentence structure varies according to function. Expository passages use long, carefully subordinated sentences to trace changes in feeling, working conditions, or social circumstances. Moments of conflict and decision shift into shorter clauses, abrupt dialogue, exclamations, and fragments. Parallel constructions and antitheses are common: well dressed versus seedy, idler versus labourer, moral fitness versus practical deception, gentleman versus shopkeeper. These oppositions reinforce the story’s concern with the disparity between appearance and reality. Punctuation is expressive but controlled, with dashes marking hesitation or evasion, semicolons organising analytical prose, and exclamation marks conveying indignation, delight, or theatrical self-presentation.

Dialogue is the principal means of dramatisation and social characterisation. Starkey speaks in commands, accusations, and manipulative euphemisms; his earlier promise of partnership and improved terms is exposed as calculated exploitation. Topham’s speech changes with circumstance. He begins terse and resentful, but when impersonating Starkey before Wigmore he adopts expansive professional assurances—“my dear sir,” “competent aid,” and “no doubt whatever”—that mimic the bland commercial rhetoric he despises. Wigmore’s speech is deferential, repetitive, hesitant, and emotionally transparent. His frequent use of “sir,” his self-corrections, and his pauses reveal both social insecurity and fundamental sincerity. The slight dialect marker “yoursel” and references to his west-country accent localise him without turning him into caricature.

The tonal movement is from grim domestic realism to comic opportunity and finally to morally ambiguous farce. Topham is initially presented as an exploited, humiliated worker, and the sixpence becomes a concentrated symbol of his dependence. Wigmore’s arrival transforms the plot: his naïve ambition offers Topham an escape, but also tempts him into impersonation and fraud. The comedy depends on dramatic irony, especially the contrast between Wigmore’s reverence for “Mr. Starkey” and the reader’s knowledge that he is speaking to the assistant. It also arises from Topham’s rapid adaptation to the role of the very charlatan he resents. His internal cry of “Ass! I always undervalue myself” turns a potentially solemn negotiation into self-mocking social comedy.

Characterisation is mixed rather than purely schematic. Starkey is treated with open satirical hostility, yet Topham is not idealised as his innocent opposite. He is industrious, educated, and genuinely capable of teaching Wigmore, but also opportunistic, deceptive, and increasingly adept at self-exculpation. Wigmore is comic in his aspiration to become a curate for the sake of family respectability, yet his kindness, perseverance, and wounded paternal pride give the comedy pathos. This balance prevents the story from becoming either a simple revenge fantasy or a harsh exposure of social pretension.

The central thematic vocabulary concerns work, money, education, respectability, gentility, and professional identity. Social rank is shown as performative and unstable: Starkey’s degree and advertised authority conceal incompetence; Topham’s damaged reputation conceals real ability; Wigmore’s successful trade seems shameful to him beside the prestige of the Church. Education functions both as a genuine means of self-improvement and as a commodity sold through inflated promises. Clerical aspiration is likewise treated ambivalently, at once sincere, socially vain, and commercially exploitable.

Structurally, the story is linear and tightly causal. The first two chapters establish oppression and desperation; the third introduces the accidental opportunity; the fourth completes the negotiation and supplies a brisk retrospective resolution. Backstory is inserted only where it clarifies present motives. The decisive encounter unfolds largely as a dialogue scene, allowing suspense to grow through Wigmore’s reluctance to name his ambition and Topham’s gradual recognition of its value. The ending accelerates through summary, letters, confession, and retrospective explanation, then closes on an ironic epigram rather than a dramatic climax.

Overall, the style is best described as socially observant realism sharpened by satirical omniscience. Its distinguishing features are economical physical detail, psychologically analytical narration, class-marked dialogue, balanced syntax, understated irony, and an ending that leaves moral judgement suspended between justice and fraud. The prose invites sympathy for weakness and hardship while remaining alert to vanity, hypocrisy, and the human talent for turning self-interest into a consoling moral narrative.

generation.response_text:
### I

Two men sat on opposite sides of a table which was too large for the room and too small for the work upon it.

Rudolph Starkey, proprietor of the Imperial Collegiate Correspondence Bureau, wore a velvet smoking-jacket, a clean collar, and slippers embroidered with tarnished gold thread. His chair was tilted backward; one hand lay in his pocket, while the other held a cigarette from which he drew at intervals expressive less of enjoyment than of grievance. Before him stood a cup of cold coffee and an unopened newspaper.

Topham had no cigarette, and his coat was shiny at the elbows. He bent over a pile of exercise-books with a wooden penholder between his fingers. On his right were letters awaiting tactful answers; on his left, manuscripts requiring correction; beneath his elbow, half concealed by a grammar, lay the proof of an advertisement announcing that personal attention was bestowed by Mr. Rudolph Starkey, M.A., upon every student entrusted to his distinguished care.

“Have you finished the commercial arithmetic?” asked Starkey.

“No.”

“You said you would finish it this morning.”

“I said I might.”

“Your tone is quite unnecessary.”

Topham made no answer. He had discovered, after nine months of experiment, that silence was the only reply which Starkey could neither misquote nor charge with insolence.

Starkey picked up the advertisement and read a line of it with approval.

“‘A unique method, combining the ripe scholarship of the university with the practical requirements of modern life.’ That is good. I wrote that, I think.”

“You dictated ‘a good method.’”

“The conception was mine.”

“The adjectives were mine.”

“My dear fellow, a business man cannot stop to divide hairs over literary trifles. What matters is the directing intelligence.”

The directing intelligence yawned and reached for the newspaper.

Almost all the business of the Imperial Collegiate Correspondence Bureau was performed by Topham. He answered inquiries, prepared lessons, corrected papers, composed testimonials, devised courses, kept the accounts when there were accounts to keep, and pacified those pupils whose faith had not survived six months of Mr. Starkey’s personal attention. Starkey supplied a degree, a name with an academic sound, and that confidence which comes naturally to a man who has never considered the possibility of his own inadequacy.

He was not wholly idle, for complete idleness demands a certain strength of purpose. He began many things, spoiled some, abandoned most, and complained of the ingratitude of the world toward strenuous men. He did everything by portions, and resented the poverty of the total. If a pupil left, it was because education had fallen into contempt; if a creditor called, it was because commerce had become rapacious; if Topham objected to working fourteen hours a day without wages, it was because educated men no longer possessed loyalty.

Topham had once possessed more than loyalty. He had possessed prospects. He had been well taught, had read widely, and had seemed likely to take an honourable place in a profession which rewards discretion more regularly than intelligence. Then had come a quarrel, a reckless letter, a public accusation which he could not prove and would not withdraw. The accusation may have been true; truth, unsupported by documents, is among the least negotiable forms of property. His friends regretted him, his acquaintances avoided him, and the institution which had employed him discovered a moral objection to continuing to do so.

For a while he had lived by occasional teaching. Then the teaching became more occasional and the meals less so. When Starkey found him, he offered friendship, partnership, and an immediate improvement in circumstances. The friendship proved imperative, the partnership prospective, and the improvement consisted of a bed in the attic and as much food as Starkey’s landlady could be persuaded to provide without payment.

A gentleman who has been poor for a week speaks lightly of the open road; one who has been poor for a year understands the value of a roof.

Thus Topham remained.

Starkey turned a page of the newspaper.

“I shall require five shillings this afternoon,” he said.

“There are three and ninepence in the cash-box.”

“There ought to be more.”

“There would be, if Mrs. Pelling of Bath had paid her second instalment.”

“You should have written firmly.”

“I wrote three times.”

“Then you should have written effectively.”

Topham put down his pen.

“You may write the fourth letter yourself.”

Starkey stared at him. “Really, Topham, your temper is becoming intolerable. I have treated you as a friend.”

“You have treated me as a clerk who cannot give notice.”

“You eat at my expense.”

“At your landlady’s.”

“And you occupy a room for which I am responsible.”

“For which you are three weeks in arrears.”

Starkey lowered his chair with a thump. Conflict disturbed him when it ceased to be one-sided.

“I refuse to discuss money in this sordid fashion. You know that when the bureau develops—as it must develop—you will benefit. I have always intended that.”

“The bureau has developed. It has developed from two pupils to thirty-seven.”

“Exactly.”

“And my benefit has developed from supper to supper and breakfast to no breakfast.”

Starkey’s face expressed injury. He liked gratitude when he could obtain it cheaply, and regarded the want of it as a personal fraud.

“You asked me for sixpence yesterday,” he said.

“I did.”

“And I lent it.”

“Yes.”

“That does not suggest oppression.”

Topham looked toward the mantelpiece, where the sixpenny piece lay beside a cracked ink-bottle. He had borrowed it to buy tobacco, and had not bought the tobacco. The coin had become too valuable to spend and too humiliating to touch.

“No,” he said. “It suggests generosity.”

Starkey, missing the irony, was mollified.

“I knew you would see matters reasonably. Now get on with the Reverend Merton’s Latin. His examination is in a fortnight, and he is most dissatisfied.”

“So he ought to be. You promised to teach him Latin in six weeks.”

“An energetic man could learn it in six weeks.”

“Then why did you never learn it?”

Starkey rose. “I am going out.”

“So I inferred.”

“I have an important appointment.”

Topham glanced at the slippers.

“I shall change my shoes.”

He did so, after a leisurely search for a bootlace. At the door he paused.

“If anyone calls, I am engaged at the university.”

“You have not been inside the university for twelve years.”

“That is beside the point. A professional establishment must preserve appearances.”

The door closed behind him. Topham heard his steps descend, heard a dispute with the landlady in the passage, and then heard the front door slam.

He sat alone among the papers. The mantel clock ticked with officious precision. From the street came the cry of a seller of flowers; from below, the landlady’s voice explaining to someone that promises were not legal tender.

Topham picked up the sixpence, turned it over, and put it into his waistcoat pocket.

For ten minutes he corrected a clergyman’s Latin. Then he rested his forehead in his hands.

He was thirty-four, hungry, able to translate three dead languages, and afraid of the rain.

### II

At twelve o’clock the landlady entered without knocking.

“There’s a gentleman asking for Mr. Starkey.”

“Mr. Starkey is out.”

“So I told him. He says he has come from a distance.”

“Then he has had a wasted journey.”

“He looks like a man who can pay.”

This final circumstance altered the case. Mrs. Dawlish distrusted education, but she respected solvency wherever she could recognise it.

“Show him up,” said Topham.

The visitor who entered was a broad, healthy man of perhaps fifty-five, dressed with a care which did not conceal the provincial origin of his clothes. His boots were excellent but heavy; his gloves new and uncomfortable. A gold watch-chain crossed a waistcoat of generous dimensions, and a small silver fruit-knife hung among its seals. His face was ruddy, open, and troubled. He carried a tightly rolled umbrella and a parcel wrapped in brown paper.

“Mr. Starkey, sir?”

Topham was about to deny the name. Then he observed the parcel, the boots, and the deferential anxiety with which the stranger awaited his answer.

A denial would send the man away. An explanation would lead to questions. Besides, Topham had written every letter which bore Starkey’s signature for the past eight months.

“I am Mr. Starkey,” he said.

The words, once spoken, produced less alarm than he had expected. Respectability often rests upon no stronger foundation than a prompt answer.

The visitor brightened.

“Wigmore, sir—Abraham Wigmore. You may recall the name.”

“Certainly. Elementary History, English Composition, and Introductory Latin.”

“That is me, sir. That is—I am the pupil.”

Topham recalled him well. Mr. Wigmore wrote on thick, scented paper and formed his capital letters with painful magnificence. He had once translated *agricola* as “a gentleman farmer,” and had apologised in three pages.

“I did not expect a personal visit,” said Topham, acquiring Starkey’s most professional manner with surprising ease.

“No, sir. I hope it is not a liberty. I had business in town, and I thought—being so near, or near enough—that I might ask your advice private.”

“Pray sit down.”

Wigmore sat upon the edge of the chair and placed the parcel on his knees.

“A little something from my own establishment,” he said. “Pears. Not common pears, sir. I picked them out myself.”

“That was very kind.”

“I am in fruit.”

“So I understood.”

“Wholesale and retail. Wigmore and Son, though the son is no longer with us, poor boy. Fever, six years ago.”

“I am sorry.”

“Thank you, sir. Business is good. I cannot complain of business. Three shops, two vans, and the warehouse. A man might do worse.”

Topham agreed that a man might. Indeed, looking at the visitor’s substantial coat and thinking of the empty cupboard downstairs, he felt that a man very often did.

“But there are things,” Wigmore continued, “which business does not give.”

“Leisure?”

“Standing, sir.”

He uttered the word softly, as if it belonged to a vocabulary which he had paid to enter.

Topham waited.

“I have two daughters. Good girls, both of them. I deny nobody that. Emily married Mr. Chalfont, who is in the law—not a solicitor exactly, but connected with legal affairs. Rose married a gentleman whose uncle is a canon. They have moved among different people since.”

“Different from fruiterers?”

Wigmore flushed.

“I do not say better. No, sir, I will not say better. There are honest men behind counters and rogues in drawing-rooms, as my poor wife used to tell me. Still, there is a manner. An education. A man feels it.”

“And your daughters have made you feel it?”

The question was direct, but Wigmore did not resent it. Sincere people are often grateful for the wound which saves them the labour of making an incision.

“They are affectionate,” he said quickly. “They write. Emily sends a hamper at Christmas, though what a fruiterer wants with preserved ginger I cannot say. Rose has asked me to visit, more than once. But when her husband’s friends are there she calls the business ‘importing.’ Last summer, at the seaside, I heard her tell a lady that I had retired.”

“Had you?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you correct her?”

Wigmore looked down at his umbrella. “It would have embarrassed her.”

There was a short silence. Topham’s first amusement had disappeared. Vanity in a prosperous man may be comic, but a father’s shame before his children has an inconvenient dignity.

“That is why I took up the course,” Wigmore said. “A man cannot alter his beginnings, but he may improve his ending. I have worked. Perhaps not well.”

“You have worked very diligently.”

The pupil’s face shone at this scrap of praise.

“I knew you would speak honest, sir. Your remarks in the margins have been strict, but helpful. ‘This sentence possesses enthusiasm rather than grammar’—that was yours.”

“It was.”

“I copied it into a book.”

Topham felt a discomfort which was almost remorse, though he had not yet profited by the deception.

“What exactly do you wish to ask me?”

Wigmore shifted in his chair.

“It is difficult.”

“Most important questions are difficult until they are stated.”

“That is like one of your printed lessons.”

“It may become one.”

The pupil laughed obediently, then grew solemn.

“I want to leave the business.”

“Can you afford to?”

“Yes. The warehouse is worth something, and Perkins, my manager, would take the shops. I have put money by. Not a fortune, but comfortable. Two thousand a year, perhaps a shade under after all is settled.”

Topham’s hand moved involuntarily toward the frayed cuff of his coat.

“And after leaving business?”

“That is what I require your opinion upon. Whether a man of my age, if he laboured under competent direction—daily, I mean, not merely by post—might make himself fit for a position.”

“What position?”

Wigmore’s ruddy face became redder.

“It may sound foolish.”

“Say it.”

“A curate.”

Topham stared.

Wigmore hurried on. “Not a rector, sir. I know my place. I would not expect a living, nor a grand pulpit, nor anything of that kind. But a curate in some quiet parish—a useful man. Visiting the sick, reading the lessons, helping the poor. I have always respected the Church. My wife’s father was a verger.”

“And you wish to be ordained?”

“If it could be managed.”

“For the sake of your daughters?”

“Not altogether.” He hesitated. “Not more than partly. I should like Rose to say, ‘My father is in the Church,’ without lowering her voice. I admit that. But I have other reasons. A man who has spent thirty-five years persuading people to buy sound apples knows something of human nature. There are lonely people in back streets. I have seen them. I have given fruit away when it would not keep, but that is not the same as giving comfort.”

It was an odd mixture of social ambition, wounded affection, practical benevolence, and ignorance. Yet mixtures are the usual condition of human motives; purity is claimed chiefly by those who have not examined theirs.

Topham leaned back.

“The difficulties would be considerable.”

“I expected that.”

“Your Latin is weak.”

“Very weak.”

“Your Greek does not exist.”

“No, sir.”

“Your history is uncertain, your composition heavy, and your theology at present confined to good intentions.”

Wigmore received each blow with a grave nod.

“But,” Topham continued, “you are industrious. You accept correction. You have sufficient means to obtain books and competent aid. With intensive private tuition, and if the necessary authorities viewed your age and circumstances favourably, I see no reason for despair.”

“Then you think it possible?”

“I think many men have entered professions with less ability and worse motives.”

Wigmore rose in his excitement, upsetting the umbrella.

“I knew it! I said to myself, ‘Go to Mr. Starkey. He will not flatter you. He will say yes or no.’ And you say yes!”

“I said possible.”

“Possible is yes with work attached.”

Topham looked at him sharply. The fruiterer was not such a fool as his grammar suggested.

“Where would you study?” he asked.

“At my house. I have a good room over the garden, quite separate. Quiet. My housekeeper is an excellent cook. I thought perhaps there might be a gentleman—a university gentleman—who would live in and direct me.”

Topham heard the mantel clock. He heard also, with remarkable distinctness, Starkey’s voice ordering five shillings, Mrs. Dawlish demanding rent, and the rain which had not yet begun striking upon an imaginary pavement under which he might shortly sleep.

“A resident tutor,” he said.

“Yes, sir.”

“That would be expensive.”

“I am prepared for expense.”

“What sum had you considered?”

Wigmore named one.

Topham preserved the calm of Mr. Rudolph Starkey, M.A., but the impoverished Topham within him sprang up and shouted at his own stupidity. He had spent months believing himself cheap because a cheap man had told him so.

“The sum,” he said slowly, “might secure a junior tutor. Your case requires experience, patience, and a breadth of instruction not commonly found in one person.”

“I could increase it.”

He named a second sum.

Topham folded his hands.

“And an allowance for books?”

“Of course.”

“Travelling expenses?”

“Certainly.”

“A month’s salary in advance is customary.”

“If you say so, sir.”

The ease of it made Topham suspicious. Years of poverty teach a man that every open door is likely to belong to someone else’s house.

“You would entrust the selection to me?”

“Entirely.”

“I may know a suitable person.”

“Could he begin soon?”

“Very soon.”

“Within a month?”

“Within a day.”

Wigmore blinked.

Topham stood and went to the window. Below, a butcher’s boy splashed through the first drops of rain. Across the street, a clerk in a neat overcoat entered a dining-room where the legend “Ordinary, One Shilling” was displayed behind clean glass.

He had only to remain silent and return to the Reverend Merton’s Latin. He had only to continue being honest for the benefit of a man who lived by dishonest promises. There are moments when principle speaks clearly; unfortunately, hunger speaks at the same time.

He turned.

“The gentleman I have in mind has suffered a reverse,” he said. “His qualifications are excellent, but certain circumstances have prejudiced conventional employers against him.”

Wigmore nodded sympathetically. “Drink?”

“No.”

“Money trouble?”

“No.”

“A woman?”

“Nothing so respectable. He told the truth at an inconvenient moment.”

“Then I should like him.”

“You have not seen him.”

“I take your recommendation.”

Topham almost laughed.

“My dear sir, confidence is admirable, but must be tempered by judgement.”

“That is what I pay you for.”

For once, commercial rhetoric had answered itself.

### III

The arrangement was completed in less than half an hour. Mr. Wigmore drew a cheque at the table, blowing upon the ink before he folded it. He wrote the amount with the care of a man to whom money was important but not mysterious.

“The tutor’s name?” he asked.

“Topham.”

“Christian name?”

“Edmund.”

“Mr. Edmund Topham.” Wigmore repeated it as though committing a lesson to memory. “And you answer for him?”

“I answer for his teaching.”

“That is enough.”

“No,” said Topham, more sharply than he intended. “It may not be. You should understand that he is proud, impatient under injustice, and not always scrupulous when driven into a corner.”

Wigmore considered this.

“Will he work?”

“Yes.”

“Will he teach me honest?”

“Yes.”

“Then we will try each other. A man must be judged where he stands, not where he stumbled. You said something like that in Lesson Seven.”

Topham had, in fact, invented the sentence to fill a blank space at the bottom of a page.

“When do you return home?” he asked.

“By the four-ten.”

“Mr. Topham will accompany you.”

“Today?”

“Today.”

Wigmore’s delight was almost boyish.

“Then we shall begin tomorrow! Greek, perhaps?”

“English syntax.”

“Ah. Yes. We must not run before we can walk.”

“Nor seek ordination before we can punctuate.”

Wigmore laughed again. He tied up the parcel of pears, then pushed it across the table.

“You keep those, sir. With my thanks.”

“I shall.”

At the door he paused.

“You will continue to supervise the course, Mr. Starkey?”

“In a sense.”

“That comforts me. I have come to depend on your judgement.”

When he had gone downstairs, Topham remained motionless. The cheque lay before him; beside it stood the pears, golden beneath their brown wrapping. Both looked improbable.

Then action took possession of him.

He went first to the bank indicated by Wigmore, presented the cheque, and received notes and gold. The clerk counted the money without asking whether Topham deserved it. Banks, unlike moralists, are satisfied by signatures.

He next purchased a serviceable portmanteau, two shirts, a collar, and a second-hand coat which fitted him sufficiently well to suggest that it had once belonged to a thinner optimist. He paid Mrs. Dawlish what Starkey owed her on his behalf, though she protested that half would do until Saturday.

“Are you coming into money, Mr. Topham?” she asked.

“I am going out of Mr. Starkey.”

“That is much the same thing.”

He packed his books, his razors, and the few letters which survived from better years. The whole of his possessions entered the portmanteau without argument. On the table he placed a note addressed to Starkey.

He wrote it twice. The first version was eloquent, accusatory, and therefore dangerous. The second contained four lines.

> Dear Starkey,—I have obtained employment elsewhere and leave today. I enclose the sixpence which you lent me yesterday, with sincere gratitude for all the generosity it represents. You will find the Reverend Merton’s exercise corrected to page sixteen. The remainder may afford exercise to you.  
>   
> E. Topham.

He laid the sixpence upon the paper.

After reflection, he added another envelope, stamped and addressed to the Imperial Collegiate Correspondence Bureau. Inside it was a letter purporting to come from Wigmore.

> Sir,—Owing to a sudden and serious failure of health, I regret that I am compelled to abandon my studies indefinitely. I must therefore request that no further lessons be sent and no further fees charged. With thanks for past attention, yours faithfully, Abraham Wigmore.

Topham imitated the pupil’s laborious capitals, his unnecessary commas, and the flourish beneath his name. The forgery was excellent. Education had at last produced a practical result.

He posted the letter at a box near the station.

At three-forty he met Wigmore under the clock. The fruiterer had bought an evening paper and appeared to have read none of it.

“You are Mr. Topham?”

“I am.”

Wigmore examined him with frank curiosity.

“Mr. Starkey described you.”

“Did he?”

“He spoke highly of your ability.”

“That was handsome of him.”

“He also said you had met with injustice.”

“On that subject he is well informed.”

Something in the reply puzzled Wigmore, but the platform bell rang before he could pursue it. They entered a second-class compartment. Wigmore talked for forty miles, chiefly about his house, his daughters, the late Mrs. Wigmore, and the proper storage of citrus fruit. Topham listened with a patience which surprised him. A full stomach, a railway ticket, and a definite destination had already improved his character.

At the junction Wigmore produced sandwiches.

“Ham,” he said. “I hope you do not object.”

“I object to very little that is edible.”

“You have been badly placed, perhaps?”

“I have been placed where meals were treated as an encouragement to idleness.”

Wigmore looked at him, then handed over a second sandwich without comment.

They reached his town after dark. A dog-cart waited outside the station. Twenty minutes later they entered a square red house behind high laurels, with lamps burning in three windows and a smell of roast beef in the hall.

The room over the garden contained a broad desk, two armchairs, shelves newly cleared for books, and a blackboard which Wigmore had ordered in anticipation. A fire burned brightly. On the desk stood fresh ink, a box of pens, and a silver bell.

“For anything you require,” said Wigmore.

Topham touched the bell but did not ring it.

“What I require first is a timetable.”

His pupil beamed.

### IV

For three days Topham postponed his confession. Cowardice played some part in the delay, but practical considerations played more. He wished to begin work before Wigmore could decide that no work was possible under a liar.

At eight each morning they read English prose. At ten they took Latin. After luncheon they walked, and Topham required his pupil to describe accurately what he had seen, an exercise which Wigmore considered childish until he discovered that he could not do it. In the evening they studied history or Scripture. Wigmore attacked irregular verbs with the resolution of a man who had once built a business from a barrow and nine shillings. He forgot slowly, remembered obstinately, and never pretended to understand.

On the fourth evening, after an hour spent upon the ablative absolute, Topham closed the book.

“There is something I must tell you.”

Wigmore’s face fell. “You are leaving?”

“No.”

“Then it cannot be the worst.”

“It may appear worse.”

Topham walked to the fireplace.

“When you called in London, the man to whom you spoke was not Rudolph Starkey.”

Wigmore stared.

“It was you?”

“Yes.”

“You said you were him.”

“Yes.”

“And recommended yoursel.”

“Yes.”

The west-country turn of the last word, usually softened by effort, emerged under agitation.

Topham explained. He omitted neither the impersonation nor the forged letter; necessity may excuse a deception to the deceiver, but confession which conceals the profitable portions is merely a second fraud.

Wigmore listened with his hands upon his knees.

When the account was finished, he rose and walked twice around the room. Then he stopped before the blackboard, upon which *Caesar, having crossed the river,* remained written in chalk.

“This Mr. Starkey,” he said, “did he teach me anything?”

“He did not teach you. I prepared the lessons and corrected the papers.”

“And the remarks in the margins?”

“Mine.”

“‘Enthusiasm rather than grammar’?”

“Mine.”

“And he kept the money?”

“Yes.”

“What did he pay you?”

“Food and lodging, when available.”

Wigmore’s astonishment hardened into anger.

“Then he is a rogue.”

“He would call himself a man of ideas.”

“I have met the sort in business. They call the cart an organisation and forget to pay the horse.”

Topham smiled despite himself.

“You do not propose to send me away?”

“I have not decided that.”

“That is reasonable.”

“Do not hurry me, sir. I am angry, and I do not always think best when angry.”

Topham waited.

Wigmore went to the window, though the curtains were drawn. After several moments he said, “You lied to me.”

“I did.”

“You took my money under a false name.”

“Yes.”

“But you are the man who did the work I paid for before?”

“Yes.”

“And you can teach what I need?”

“If anyone can.”

“That sounds proud.”

“It is meant to.”

Wigmore turned. “Then we will settle it this way. You will remain for one month. At the end of the month, if I am satisfied, you remain longer. If not, you go—with the month paid, because I agreed it. But there will be no more false names and no more letters written as me.”

“Agreed.”

“And if Mr. Starkey comes here?”

“He may.”

“What shall I say?”

“The truth.”

Wigmore’s eyes brightened.

“I have often wished to say the truth to a gentleman with a degree.”

Starkey did not come. He wrote six letters, however: two imperious, two conciliatory, one threatening legal proceedings, and one suggesting that Topham return as a partner on revised terms. Topham answered none of them.

The Imperial Collegiate Correspondence Bureau declined rapidly. The Reverend Merton failed his examination; Mrs. Pelling of Bath requested the return of her fees; three pupils received identical essays upon the causes of the French Revolution, though one was studying bookkeeping. Starkey attributed these reverses to Topham’s treachery, never reflecting that a business destroyed by the departure of an unpaid subordinate may have mistaken the identity of its proprietor.

At Wigmore’s house matters advanced more slowly and more soundly.

The pupil never became a classical scholar. Greek verbs oppressed him, and the finer distinctions of theology sometimes appeared to him less reasonable than the grading of oranges. Yet he learned. His sentences lost weight without losing substance; his reading acquired intelligence; his charity, which had formerly been impulsive, became informed. Topham took him into poor streets and showed him that benevolence requires attention as well as a basket. Wigmore, in return, taught Topham that regular meals do not necessarily corrupt the intellect.

The daughters heard of the plan with alarm. Emily wrote that the Church was not a refuge for persons tired of commerce. Rose came in person, accompanied by her husband, and asked whether her father had considered the social difficulties.

“I have,” said Wigmore. “They are the reason I began, but not the reason I shall finish.”

Topham, overhearing from the adjoining room, allowed himself a small smile.

Whether Wigmore would ultimately be ordained remained uncertain. There were examinations, authorities, and prejudices still to be encountered; institutions which willingly accept a young fool often scrutinise an elderly man of sense. But a sympathetic clergyman was found, a course was arranged, and the former fruiterer persevered with a steadiness which made predictions unsafe.

Topham also prospered. He became better dressed, less bitter, and, when not reminded of Starkey, almost honest in his estimate of mankind. He knew that his escape had begun in fraud, and at times the knowledge troubled him. At such moments he reflected that he had rescued himself from servitude, delivered Wigmore from an incompetent impostor, punished a scoundrel, and placed a sincere man upon the road to useful work.

He further reflected that, had he told the truth at once, none of these excellent consequences would have occurred.

Such arguments gave him considerable peace.

### The Museum of Lost Hours

On the morning the clocks forgot eleven, Mara Venn was repairing a silver pocket watch in the back room of her shop.

It was a delicate thing, no wider than a plum, engraved with a heron standing among reeds. Its owner, a retired judge, had complained that it lost seven minutes each day. Mara had found the usual symptoms—dust in the movement, dried oil, a bent tooth on the escape wheel—but as she leaned close to the mechanism, tweezers poised, every clock in the shop stopped.

The silence was enormous.

Mara looked up.

On the wall, thirty-seven clock faces showed thirty-seven different versions of the same moment: three minutes past eleven. The tall walnut grandfather clock near the door had halted with its pendulum at the peak of its swing. The cuckoo in the blue Bavarian clock had thrust open its tiny door but had not emerged.

Outside, a delivery truck stood motionless in the street. A pigeon hung above its roof with wings spread, perfectly still. Rain glittered in the air like strings of glass beads.

Mara’s hand began to shake.

Then the bell over the front door rang.

A little girl stepped into the shop.

She wore a yellow coat, green boots, and a red woolen scarf wound twice around her neck. Rain did not touch her. She closed the door behind her, studied the room, and said, “Are you Mara Venn?”

“That depends,” Mara replied.

“On what?”

“On whether you’re here to pay a bill.”

The girl considered this. “No.”

“Then I’m Mara Venn.”

“My name is Elianor.”

“Elianor what?”

“Just Elianor.”

Mara put down her tweezers. “Do your parents know where you are?”

“No. They haven’t known for quite a long time.”

The girl reached inside her coat and produced a square of black paper. At least, Mara thought it was paper until it flexed like cloth and shone like polished stone. A message had been written across it in pale gold ink.

MARA VENN, CLOCKMAKER  
ADMISSION FOR ONE  
THE MUSEUM OF LOST HOURS  
ELEVEN O’CLOCK SHARP

Below the words was an address Mara knew well.

Number Nine, Bellweather Lane.

“That’s impossible,” she said.

“So people keep telling me.”

Bellweather Lane had once run behind the old railway station. It had been destroyed in a fire twenty-two years earlier, when Mara was ten. Number Nine had been her childhood home.

She turned the card over. There was no writing on the back.

“Who gave you this?”

“The Curator.”

“Who is the Curator?”

“You’ll know him when you see him.”

“I’m not going anywhere with you.”

Elianor glanced at the frozen clocks. “You already are.”

The cuckoo clock clicked.

Mara turned toward it. The bird had finally emerged, but it did not call. Its small wooden head pointed toward a door at the rear of the shop.

There had never been a door there before.

It was narrow, painted dark green, with a tarnished brass number fixed at eye level.

9.

Mara stood so quickly that her stool toppled.

Elianor opened the door.

Beyond it lay Bellweather Lane.

Not the lane as it appeared now, buried beneath the foundations of a supermarket, but as Mara remembered it from childhood. Red-brick houses leaned together beneath smoking chimneys. Wet laundry stirred overhead. At the far end, the station clock rose above the rooftops.

Its hands showed eleven.

Mara stepped to the threshold. The air smelled of coal smoke, rain, and the cinnamon buns her mother used to bake on Sundays.

Her mother had been dead for twenty-two years.

“This isn’t real,” Mara whispered.

Elianor shrugged. “Real is a word people use when they want things to stay put.”

Then she crossed the threshold.

Mara could have closed the door. She could have returned to her workbench and waited for the clocks to resume. She could have told herself that grief, lack of sleep, and the fumes from cleaning solvent had created the entire vision.

Instead, she followed.

The door swung shut behind her.

Number Nine stood halfway down the lane, though it was not the house Mara remembered. The front windows were too tall, and the roof rose through the clouds. Gargoyles crouched along the gutters, each holding an hourglass in its mouth. Above the entrance, silver letters spelled:

THE MUSEUM OF LOST HOURS  
PLEASE LEAVE UMBRELLAS, WEAPONS, AND REGRETS AT THE DESK

Elianor climbed the steps.

Inside, the entrance hall stretched farther than the building could have contained. Thousands of clocks covered the walls. Some ticked forward; others backward. One had thirteen numbers. Another had no hands, only a tiny painted ship sailing around its face.

An elderly man waited behind a marble desk. He wore a plum-colored suit, white gloves, and spectacles with octagonal lenses. His hair was as orderly as typeset letters.

“Miss Venn,” he said. “You are late.”

“The clocks stopped.”

“That is no excuse in a place like this.”

“You sent the card?”

“I did.”

“Why?”

He looked at Elianor. “You did not tell her?”

“You said not to.”

“Remarkable. Someone in this building still follows instructions.”

The man came around the desk and bowed.

“Dr. Silas Vale, Curator of Misplaced Time, Keeper of Unfinished Afternoons, Registrar of Moments Too Painful to Remember.”

“Mara Venn,” she said. “Clockmaker, taxpayer, and person rapidly losing patience.”

“Excellent. Impatience is closely related to courage, though less useful at dinner parties.”

He turned and walked through a high arched doorway. “Come. We have little time, which is, regrettably, why you are here.”

Mara did not move.

Dr. Vale looked back. “Your brother is alive.”

The hall seemed to tilt.

Mara heard ticking all around her, louder and louder, until it resembled rain beating on a thousand roofs.

“My brother died in the fire.”

“So everyone believes.”

“I saw the house burn.”

“You saw fire. Human beings often mistake seeing one thing for understanding another.”

Mara crossed the hall in three strides and seized his lapels.

“If this is some kind of trick—”

“No trick.” His voice remained calm. “Your brother has been trapped in a single hour for twenty-two years.”

Elianor touched Mara’s wrist. “Let him breathe.”

Mara released the Curator.

Dr. Vale adjusted his suit. “Thank you. These lapels are original.”

He led them into the museum.

They passed through galleries no architect could have drawn. In one room, glass jars held the final minutes before people fell asleep. Soft voices drifted from them: unfinished prayers, remembered songs, promises to wake early.

In another, lost childhood summers lay folded in display cases like golden cloth. Mara saw children racing bicycles along a road bordered by wheat. She heard distant mothers calling them home.

“What is this place?” she asked.

“People lose more time than keys,” said Dr. Vale. “An hour vanishes in a hospital corridor. A year disappears inside an unhappy marriage. Whole decades are misplaced while waiting to become someone else. We collect what we can.”

“Why?”

“Because lost things are not the same as empty things.”

Elianor walked beside a row of bottles, trailing one finger across the glass.

“Did she lose time too?” Mara asked.

The girl answered before Dr. Vale could.

“I’m an exhibit.”

She pointed toward a small brass plaque on the wall.

ELIANOR VALE  
AGE: NINE  
STATUS: UNFINISHED  
DO NOT REMOVE FROM PREMISES

Mara looked from the plaque to the Curator.

“Your daughter?”

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“Later,” he said.

They reached a circular chamber with a black door at its center. The door stood alone, unsupported by any wall. Around it, twelve stone figures held lanterns.

Dr. Vale stopped.

“Behind that door is the hour between eleven and midnight on the seventh of November, twenty-two years ago. The hour of the Bellweather fire.”

Mara felt ten years old again.

She remembered smoke waking her. Her mother shouting from downstairs. Heat beneath her bare feet. Her father carrying her through a window while she screamed her brother’s name.

Jonas had been sixteen. He had gone back for Mara’s wooden music box because she had been crying about leaving it behind.

At least, that was what her father had told her.

“He died because of me,” Mara said.

“No,” said Dr. Vale. “He did not die.”

“Then open the door.”

“I cannot.”

“Why?”

“Because you locked it.”

He took a small object from his pocket.

Mara recognized it immediately: a brass winding key, darkened with age. She wore an identical one on a chain beneath her blouse. It had belonged to the mantel clock in their childhood home.

“The museum answers to acts of human will,” Dr. Vale said. “That night, at precisely eleven sixteen, you wished for the hour to stop. You wished it with the absolute conviction only a terrified child can possess.”

“I don’t remember.”

“Of course not. The wish took the memory with it.”

He gave her the key.

“Your brother heard you crying and ran toward your room. At that moment, the hour closed. Everyone outside continued forward. Jonas remained behind.”

“For twenty-two years?”

“For him, the fire has lasted forty-four minutes.”

Mara stared at the black door.

“Why didn’t you tell me before?”

“Because the door could not be opened until you had spent more years outside the hour than Jonas had lived before entering it. Time requires balance. Today, you are thirty-two years and one day old.”

“And if I open it?”

“You may bring him out.”

“May?”

Dr. Vale’s face softened.

“Lost hours resist being found.”

He nodded to the keyhole.

Mara inserted the brass key. It turned with a heavy click.

The door opened onto fire.

Heat rushed into the chamber. Beyond the threshold was the upstairs corridor of Number Nine. Wallpaper curled in the flames. Smoke crawled across the ceiling.

At the far end stood Jonas.

He looked exactly as Mara remembered: tall and thin, black hair falling into his eyes, one sleeve torn at the elbow. He held her wooden music box against his chest.

“Mara?” he shouted.

She stepped through the door.

The museum vanished behind her.

She was barefoot, small, and coughing on the floor of her childhood bedroom.

For one impossible moment, she occupied two bodies. She was thirty-two, reaching through smoke, and she was ten, curled beneath the window, wishing with all her strength that the clock would stop.

On the mantel, the brass clock read eleven sixteen.

Jonas burst into the room.

“There you are!”

He lifted the child Mara and carried her toward the window. But the scene shuddered, bent, and returned to the beginning.

Again Mara crouched beneath the window.

Again Jonas entered.

Again the clock read eleven sixteen.

The hour was repeating.

Adult Mara stood unseen in the corner while the memory performed itself. She watched Jonas lift her younger self, watched him stagger beneath falling plaster, watched him reach the window before the flames folded backward and dragged him to the doorway again.

“Jonas!”

This time he heard her.

He spun around. The child in his arms vanished.

“Mara?”

“Yes.”

He stared. “You look old.”

Despite the fire, despite the smoke and twenty-two years of grief, Mara laughed.

“You still look rude.”

He grinned. It was the same crooked grin she had seen in dreams.

Then the ceiling cracked.

“We have to go,” she said.

“Where?”

She pointed.

The black museum door stood at the end of the corridor.

They ran toward it, but with every step, the hallway stretched. Doors multiplied along both walls. Behind each one, Mara heard voices.

Her father saying, I should have gone back.

Her mother whispering Jonas’s name.

Her own voice, year after year: It was my fault.

Jonas stopped beside one of the doors.

“That’s Mum.”

“It’s not.”

“I can hear her.”

“She’s gone, Jonas.”

He turned on her angrily. “She was downstairs five minutes ago.”

“For you.”

Understanding entered his face by degrees.

“How long?” he asked.

Mara could not soften the answer.

“Twenty-two years.”

The fire dimmed around them.

Jonas leaned against the wall. He still held the music box.

“No.”

“I’m sorry.”

“No, I was just—I went upstairs, and Dad was outside, and Mum—”

“I know.”

“You left me here?”

The words struck harder than accusation because he sounded like a child.

“I didn’t know.”

“You got out?”

“Yes.”

“And Mum?”

“She died three years ago.”

He shut his eyes.

“What about Dad?”

“Fourteen years ago.”

Jonas slid to the floor.

The hallway contracted around them. Flames rose. The clock appeared on every door, all showing eleven sixteen.

A voice came from the smoke.

“You can stay.”

Their mother stood at the far end of the corridor.

She looked young and unburned, wearing her blue nightdress. One hand rested on the banister.

“My dears,” she said.

Jonas stood.

Mara grabbed his arm. “That isn’t her.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I do.”

Their mother smiled. “You can have it all again. Breakfast in the kitchen. Summer at the lake. Christmas mornings. Nothing needs to be lost.”

For one heartbeat, Mara wanted it.

She saw her father polishing his shoes by the stove. Her mother dusted flour from her hands. Jonas stole cherries from a bowl. Outside, rain tapped against the window, and every room was warm.

The lost hour opened around her like welcoming arms.

Then Mara noticed the mantel clock.

Eleven sixteen.

Even in the imagined kitchen, it never changed.

“This isn’t time,” she said. “It’s a cage.”

Her mother’s smile widened too far.

The house shook.

Mara pulled Jonas toward the museum door. He resisted.

“She’s right there!”

“No. She’s the reason we can’t leave.”

The thing wearing their mother’s face reached for him.

Jonas stepped back.

The face collapsed into ash.

They ran.

The black door drew nearer, but flames closed around it. Mara could see Elianor on the other side, her hand extended.

“Hurry!” the girl shouted.

Jonas stumbled. The music box fell and broke open.

A tune chimed through the corridor.

Mara knew it. Their mother had wound the box each night when they were small. The melody was simple, only six notes, but the fire recoiled from it.

Inside the shattered box, brass gears turned.

A tiny compartment sprang open, revealing a folded scrap of paper.

Jonas snatched it up.

Mara recognized her mother’s handwriting.

If you find this, you have taken something that does not belong to you. Put it back, Jonas.

He laughed, breathless and astonished.

“She knew me well.”

The flames surged again.

“Leave it,” Mara said.

Jonas looked at the music box. “You loved this.”

“I loved you more.”

He dropped it.

The hallway split from end to end.

They leaped through the black door as Number Nine collapsed behind them.

Mara struck the museum floor. Jonas landed beside her.

The door slammed.

For several seconds, neither moved.

Then Jonas sat up and looked around the circular chamber.

Dr. Vale stood by one of the stone figures, his face pale. Elianor was beside him.

“So,” Jonas said. “Twenty-two years?”

Mara nodded.

“Do they have food in the future?”

“Yes.”

“Good. I’m starving.”

Mara began to laugh. She could not stop. The laughter turned to sobbing, and then Jonas wrapped his arms around her.

He smelled of smoke and rain and the soap their mother used to buy.

“You really are old,” he murmured.

“You’re still rude.”

While they held each other, a crack appeared in the floor.

Dr. Vale looked down sharply.

Another crack raced up the black door. The twelve stone lantern-bearers turned their heads.

“What is happening?” Mara asked.

“The hour was closed for twenty-two years,” said the Curator. “It does not appreciate being emptied.”

The black door burst open.

Darkness poured out—not smoke, but a tide of unwitnessed moments. Mara heard alarm clocks that never rang, goodbyes never spoken, trains missed by seconds, names forgotten at deathbeds. The chamber filled with the weight of everything people had failed to keep.

Dr. Vale seized Elianor’s hand.

“To the entrance!”

They fled through the galleries.

Display cases shattered as they passed. Childhood summers spilled across the floor in waves of sunlight. Bottled dreams rose to the ceiling. Somewhere, a thousand sleepers whispered at once.

The darkness followed.

At the entrance hall, the green door to Mara’s shop stood open. Beyond it, the frozen rain still hung above the street.

“Go!” Dr. Vale shouted.

Jonas crossed first.

Mara turned to Elianor. The girl stood behind the marble desk, gripping its edge.

“Aren’t you coming?”

“I can’t leave the museum.”

“Why not?”

Elianor pointed to her plaque.

STATUS: UNFINISHED.

Dr. Vale knelt before his daughter.

“Long ago,” he said, “Elianor fell from a tree. There was one hour in which she might have lived or died. I could not bear the second possibility, so I brought the hour here before it ended.”

“You trapped her,” Mara said.

“I preserved her.”

“For how long?”

His silence answered.

Elianor looked at Mara. “One hundred and nine years.”

The darkness reached the hall. Clocks vanished inside it, their ticking silenced.

“You have to let the hour finish,” Mara said.

Dr. Vale’s composure broke.

“She may die.”

“She may live.”

“I cannot take that chance.”

Elianor touched his cheek. “Papa, you already did. You chose this instead.”

He bowed his head.

Mara understood him then. The museum had not been built to protect time. It had been built by a frightened father who could not endure what the next minute might bring.

All cages, however beautiful, were made from fear.

Dr. Vale stood and removed his octagonal spectacles.

“Very well.”

He opened a drawer in the desk and took out a green apple, perfectly preserved. One side bore the marks of a child’s teeth.

Elianor smiled.

“I wondered where that went.”

The Curator placed the apple in her hands.

At once, the museum bells began to ring.

Elianor flickered.

For an instant she wore her yellow coat. Then she appeared in a white hospital bed, blood in her hair, her father leaning over her. Sunlight trembled across a wall.

“Papa,” she whispered.

“I am here.”

She took a breath.

The darkness stopped.

Every clock in the hall struck eleven.

Elianor opened her eyes again. She was still standing, but color had entered her cheeks. The brass plaque fell from the wall and broke in two.

Dr. Vale stared at her.

“You lived,” he said.

“Apparently.”

He laughed once, like a man surprised by the sound.

The museum folded.

Galleries collapsed into doorways, doorways into clocks, clocks into single points of light. Mara grabbed Elianor with one hand and Dr. Vale with the other. Together they crossed the green threshold.

It slammed behind them.

Mara’s shop returned.

Rain struck the windows. The delivery truck rolled forward. The pigeon completed the downbeat of its wings.

Every clock began ticking.

The green door was gone.

Jonas stood in the middle of the shop, staring at a mobile phone advertisement on the side of a passing bus.

“What,” he asked slowly, “is that?”

Mara laughed.

Outside, the station clock struck twelve.

The years that followed were not easy.

Jonas had to learn that the world would not pause while he grieved. He visited two graves on a hill overlooking the river. He stood there a long time, sixteen years old and thirty-eight years late.

He learned about computers, electric cars, and coffee shops that offered eighteen kinds of milk. He refused to accept that people paid money for water in bottles. He grew older, though for the first few months he checked the mirror each morning as if aging might happen all at once.

Dr. Vale and Elianor moved into the flat above Mara’s shop. Elianor entered school under the complicated description of “previously home educated.” She disliked mathematics, excelled at running, and climbed every tree she encountered.

Her father retired from curating and began repairing clocks beside Mara. He was terrible at it. He treated each broken spring as a moral tragedy and each speck of dust as a personal insult.

The museum was never seen again.

But now and then, someone entered the shop carrying a clock that had stopped at an important moment.

A widow brought one that had frozen when her husband died.

A young man brought another that had not moved since the night he abandoned his family.

A woman with tired eyes carried in a kitchen clock and said, “I think I lost ten years somewhere.”

Mara repaired what she could.

Sometimes she opened the case, cleaned the movement, replaced a worn gear, and restored the ordinary rhythm of seconds.

Sometimes there was nothing wrong with the clock.

Then Mara would make tea, turn the sign on the door from OPEN to CLOSED, and listen.

Above her workbench hung the brass key from Number Nine. It never tarnished now. On certain mornings, just before eleven, it moved gently on its hook although no wind stirred the room.

Whenever that happened, Mara looked at her brother, older by another day, arguing with Elianor or burning toast in the back room.

She listened to the clocks.

Time passed through the shop in a thousand different voices: loud and soft, hurried and patient, none of them perfectly regular. Once, Mara had believed a good clock was one that never lost a second.

She knew better now.

A good clock did not hold time still.

It let time go.
